_comment: Claim registry (docs/RESEARCH.md). Every real-world number the game or the Learning Center states as fact has an entry. status: UNVERIFIED (not yet checked against a source: game text must say so), SOURCED (a primary source is named), CHECKED (sourced and reproduced by our own calculation or test), CONTESTED (sources disagree), REFUTED (shown wrong: kept so the correction is visible), OPEN (a research question, no answer yet), UNFEASIBLE (an idea shown not to work: taught in G9). Game knobs are not claims.

claims.claim: Share of near-Earth asteroids of 140 m and larger that have been found
claims.value: about half: 11,688 found (CNEOS, 17 Oct 2026) of an estimated 21,000 to 25,000 (NEOMOD2), so 47 to 56 percent
claims.source: CNEOS discovery statistics (cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/stats, NEA-140m, accessed 2026-10-18); Nesvorny et al. 2024, Icarus 411, 115922 (NEOMOD2, Table 3)
claims.check: Divide the CNEOS count of NEAs of 140 m and up by the population model at H <= 22. Changes with time: re-check each release. Population models differ by about 15 percent, hence "about half".

claims.claim: US goal: find 90 percent of near-Earth objects of 140 m and larger
claims.value: set in 2005 by the George E. Brown, Jr. Near-Earth Object Survey Act
claims.source: NASA Authorization Act of 2005 (Public Law 109-155), section 321
claims.check: Quote the section text.

claims.claim: Damage begins near 20 m (Chelyabinsk class)
claims.value: Chelyabinsk, 15 February 2013, about 18 to 20 m, about 0.5 Mt airburst
claims.source: Popova et al. 2013, Science 342, 1069; Brown et al. 2013, Nature 503, 238
claims.check: Read the size and energy estimates in both papers.

claims.claim: Survey limiting magnitudes and nightly sky coverage used for each network
claims.value: src/config/networks.json (vLim, pCover, eps)
claims.check: Compare each network in src/config/networks.json with its survey paper: ATLAS 30 s limit (Tonry et al. 2018, PASP 130, 064505: median about 19.1, best 19.8); Catalina G96 (Jedicke et al. 2016: about 21.2); ZTF (Bellm et al. 2019, PASP 131, 018002); Rubin single visit (Ivezic et al. 2019, ApJ 873, 111); ESA Flyeye (design 21.5, Flyeye 2.0 study goal 21.0). pCover = nightly area / accessible sky (Rubin revisits a field every 3 to 4 nights, so about 0.3 rather than 0.6). Review 2026-10-18 read ATLAS, Catalina and Flyeye; ZTF and Rubin numbers were not re-read.

claims.claim: ATLAS warning time for a 10 m and a 100 m impactor
claims.value: about one day for a 20 m rock, up to about three weeks for a 100 m rock
claims.source: University of Hawaii, ATLAS news release, 27 January 2022; Tonry 2011, PASP 123, 58 (design: about three weeks for 140 m)
claims.check: Best case with V = 19.5, albedo 0.14, zero phase, 20 km/s: about 1.9 days for 10 m, 3.9 days for 20 m, 19 days for 100 m, so the team's figures are realistic and a 10 m rock gets less. Reproduce as an upper bound with LAB_MAGNITUDE.

claims.claim: Number of asteroids discovered before they hit the Earth
claims.value: thirteen, all about 8 m or smaller (as of 24 September 2026)
claims.source: ESA NEO Coordination Centre, list of past impactors (neo.ssa.esa.int, updated 2026-09-24); the largest is 2019 MO at 4 to 8 m
claims.check: Count the NEOCC past-impactors list; re-check each release (new small impactors are found every year).

claims.claim: DART momentum enhancement factor on Dimorphos
claims.value: beta about 3.6 (2.2 to 4.9 depending on Dimorphos's density)
claims.check: Read the beta range and its density assumption.

claims.claim: DART shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos
claims.value: by about 33 minutes
claims.check: Read the measured period change and its uncertainty.

claims.claim: Content should not flash more than three times in any one second
claims.value: WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold
claims.source: W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1, success criterion 2.3.1
claims.check: Read the criterion and its general and red flash thresholds; measure our flashes against them. Measured 2026-10-18 with src/render/flashMeter.ts (WCAG 2.x general and red flash thresholds): every effect at 0 flashes in the busiest second; the hit flash is a 0.0999 luminance step, just under 0.1 (docs/WARNINGS.md item 8).

claims.claim: Deflecting a Ceres-class dwarf planet with kinetic impactors
claims.value: about 7e11 DART-class hits to change its speed by 1 cm/s
claims.source: Ceres mass 9.38e20 kg: Park et al. 2016, Nature 537, 515. DART: m 580 kg, U 6.1 km/s, beta 3.6 (D3-1).
claims.check: dp = M dv = 9.38e20 x 0.01 = 9.4e18 kg m/s; one hit gives beta m U = 3.6 x 580 x 6100 = 1.27e7 kg m/s; ratio 7.4e11. Reproduced in tests/claims.test.ts.

claims.claim: Blowing a large asteroid apart hours before it arrives
claims.value: the pieces keep almost all of the original momentum and most still hit
claims.source: Momentum conservation; the game's own fragment model (src/physics/fragment.ts, EDUCATION D4)
claims.check: Spread speed of fragments (metres per second) times hours of warning is kilometres: far less than the Earth's radius, so the cloud still hits. LAB_FRAGMENT_CLOUD shows it.

claims.claim: Is a molten-salt reactor practical in free fall?
claims.value: open: freezing in the loop, gas separation without buoyancy, corrosion and mass are the known problems
claims.check: Literature search on space molten-salt reactor studies; compare specific mass with liquid-metal designs at 1 MWe.

claims.claim: Technology readiness level today of each feasibility-study technology
claims.value: src/config/studies.json trlNow
claims.check: Date each card's TRL against a source: KRUSTY (NASA NTRS 20180001487, TRL 5 at 1 kWe; a 40 kWe unit is arguably 4); no tokamak has net gain and ITER is not operating (arguably 3); HIVE: flown parts but the swarm survey is a concept (3 to 4); droplet radiators have drop-tower tests (2 to 3). Review 2026-10-18 found the others plausible; none is sourced yet.

claims.claim: Inertial fusion at NIF produced more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target
claims.value: December 2022: about 3.15 MJ out for 2.05 MJ in; wall-plug energy far larger
claims.source: Abu-Shawareb et al. 2024, Physical Review Letters 132, 065102
claims.check: Read the reported yield and laser energy.

claims.claim: Fusion products observed in deuterated metal lattices exposed to an energetic photon beam
claims.value: NASA Glenn experiments, 2020; no net energy
claims.source: Pines et al. 2020, Physical Review C 101, 044609; Steinetz et al. 2020, Physical Review C 101, 044610
claims.check: Read both papers for the beam used and the measured products.

claims.claim: Interstellar objects seen passing through the solar system
claims.value: three: 1I/'Oumuamua (2017), 2I/Borisov (2019), 3I/ATLAS (2025)
claims.source: Meech et al. 2017, Nature 552, 378 (1I); Guzik et al. 2020, Nature Astronomy 4, 53 (2I); Minor Planet Center MPEC 2025-N12 (3I/ATLAS, July 2025)
claims.check: Read the discovery papers and the MPC circular; dates and designations.

claims.claim: Impact rate of interstellar objects of 100 m and larger on the Earth
claims.value: about one hit per 40 to 140 million years for 100 m class visitors
claims.source: Do, Tucker and Tonry 2018, ApJ Letters 855, L10 (number density about 0.2 per cubic AU for objects like 1I/'Oumuamua)
claims.check: rate = n x sigma x v with n = 0.2 au^-3, sigma = pi R^2 (1 + v_esc^2 / v^2), v 26 to 32 km/s, with and without the Sun's focusing; tests/claims.test.ts reproduces the range.

claims.claim: Hyperbolic excess speeds (relative to the Sun) of the three known interstellar visitors
claims.value: about 26 km/s (1I), 32 km/s (2I), 58 km/s (3I)
claims.source: JPL Small-Body Database osculating elements (accessed 2026-10-18): a = -1.27 au (1I), -0.851 au (2I), -0.264 au (3I); Meech et al. 2017; Guzik et al. 2020; Seligman et al. 2025, ApJ Letters (arXiv 2507.02757)
claims.check: v_inf = sqrt(mu_sun / -a); tests/claims.test.ts reproduces 26, 32 and 58 km/s from the three a values.

claims.claim: ESA's Comet Interceptor is planned to wait in space at a Sun-Earth Lagrange point for a fresh comet or an interstellar visitor
claims.value: launch planned for late 2028 or 2029, waiting in a halo orbit at Sun-Earth L2 (as of October 2026; the date is at risk)
claims.source: Jones et al. 2024, Space Science Reviews 220, 9; ESA Comet Interceptor mission page (accessed 2026-10-18)
claims.check: Re-read the ESA mission page each release: the launch is tied to Ariel's.

claims.claim: 1I/'Oumuamua was discovered after its perihelion, on its way out
claims.value: discovered 19 October 2017, about 40 days after perihelion (9 September 2017)
claims.source: MPEC 2017-U181 (perihelion 2017 September 9.4 TT; first images 18 October 2017, Pan-STARRS); JPL SBDB
claims.check: Discovery date minus perihelion date: 40 days.

claims.claim: Masses, radii and orbits of the Moon, Mars and Ganymede used for the sites
claims.source: NASA planetary fact sheets (NSSDCA); JPL planetary physical parameters
claims.check: Compare each value with the fact sheets. Review 2026-10-18: NSSDCA gives the Moon's GM as 0.00490e6 km^3/s^2 (4.90e12 m^3/s^2 to three figures); knobs MOON_MU 4.9048695e12 agrees to 0.1 percent. Mars and Ganymede were not re-read.
